headline: Metacognition is thinking about your own thinking—the skill that improves all other thinking
universal_truth: Awareness of your process lets you improve it; you can't fix what you can't see
fun_facts: The Dunning-Kruger effect shows that poor performers often can't recognize their own incompetence
Expert chess players spend more time analyzing their thinking than novices do
Writing forces metacognition—externalizing thoughts makes them visible for examination
discussion_questions: How do you know when you're thinking well versus poorly?
What thinking habits might you have that you don't notice?
How could you check your own reasoning more carefully?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: You can think about anything—but can you think about your thinking? This is metacognition: the ability to observe your own mental processes. It's the skill that lets you improve all other skills, because you can see where you're going wrong.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Most thinking is invisible—we experience conclusions but not the process that created them. Why is becoming aware of your own thinking so valuable?

options.text: When you can observe your thinking, you can catch errors, recognize biases, and deliberately improve your reasoning
options.response: Yes. Metacognition is quality control for thought. Without it, errors go unnoticed. With it, you can debug your own mental processes and upgrade them.

options.text: Thinking about thinking uses more brain power and leads to better decisions
options.response: More effort can help, but the key is the ability to observe and correct...

q1.title: Watching the Watcher
q1.script: Metacognition creates a split: one part of you thinks, another part observes. This 'watcher' can notice when you're confused, biased, or jumping to conclusions. Developing this observer is like installing a debugger in your mind.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Watching the Watcher"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Experts Examine Themselves
q2.script: Expert performers spend more time analyzing their own thinking than beginners do. After a chess game, masters analyze where their reasoning went wrong. This self-examination accelerates improvement.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Writing Externalizes Thought
q3.script: Writing forces metacognition because it makes invisible thinking visible. Once thoughts are on paper, you can examine them, question them, reorganize them. Writing isn't just recording—it's thinking made observable.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Awareness of your process lets you improve it. Metacognition teaches that you can't fix what you can't see. Develop the observer within.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 183. Tomorrow, we'll explore how to choose—decision making. Until then, pause occasionally and notice: how am I thinking right now?
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Thinking Journal - Observe Your Mind
growTrack.activity: After making a decision or solving a problem today, write a few sentences about how you thought. What information did you use? What did you assume? Where were you uncertain? This metacognitive practice makes invisible thinking visible.
